If you do not get up, you scamp,
there will be trouble in this camp.
Do I have to let you sleep
while I cook your board and keep?
That's a pretty way to act--
Do you hear me, Lias--you?

Better if I come across this floor
you won't find any time to snooze.
Daylight is all shining in
while you sleep—that's a sin!
Isn't the candlelight enough
to burn out without a snuff,
but you go through the morning too
burning up the daylight as well?

Lias, don't you hear me call?
No use turning towards the wall;
I can hear that mattress squeak;
don't you hear me when I speak?
This clock has struck six already—
Call in and bring me those sticks!
Oh, you down, sir; huh, you down—
Look here, do not dare to frown.

sae_mgt_text:
If there is anything that really irks me,
And just gets me out of sorts,
Till I want to tear off my coat,
So as to roar and tear and gloat,
It's to see some ignorant white man
Stealing that audacious skin—
When he wants to cook a possum,
Tearing off the possum's skin.

Why there is no use in talking,
It just hurts me to the heart,
Full to see those foolish people
Throwing away the finest part.
Oh, that skin is just as tender
And as juicy as can be;
I know all about the creature—
Hide and hair—I don't want to talk to you!

Possum skin is just like pork skin;
Just you singe and scrape it down,
Take a good sharp knife and score it,
Then you bake it good and brown.
Huh-uh! honey, you're so happy
That your thoughts are almost a sin
When you're sitting there chewing
On that possum's crackling skin.

White folks think they know about eating,
And I reckon that they do;
Sometimes get a little idea
Of a middling dish or two;
But there isn't a thing they know of
That I reckon can't be beat,
When we sit down at the table
To an unskinned possum's meat!

sae_mgt_text:
Haven't you seen my Mandy Lou,
    Is it true?
How have you been from day to day,
    I say?
That you claim you never've seen
    This hideous queen
Walking round from field to street
    Smiling sweet?

Slender as a sapling tree;
    Seems to me
When the wind blows from the bay
    She just sways
Like a regular sapling does
    If it grows
Straight and graceful, without a limb,
    Sweet and slim.

Brownier than the vulture's wing,
    And she sings
Like he makes his warble ring
    In the spring;
But she surely beats the vulture,
    Hear me, hush:
When she sings, her teeth can show
    White as snow.

Eyes as big and round and bright
    As the light
What the moon gives in the prime
    Harvest time.
And her hair a woolly skein,
    Black and plain.
Holds you with a natural twist
    Close to bliss.

Tender hands that make your own
    Feel like stone;
Easy stepping, blessed feet,
    Small and sweet.
Haven't you seen my Mandy Lou,
    Is it true?
Look at her before she's gone,
    Then pass on!

sae_mgt_text:
I feel kind of lonesome in my little room tonight,
And my mind has lost the minutes and the miles,
While it takes me back, flying to the country of delight,
Where the Chesapeake goes grumbling or with smiles.

Oh, the old plantation's calling to me, Come, come back,
Here's the place full enough for you to labor and rest.
'Cause my sandy roads are gleaming while the city ways are black;
Come back, honey, since your country home is best.

I know the moon is shining down upon the Eastern shore,
And the bay is saying "Howdy" to the land,
And the folks are all sitting out around the cabin door,
With their feet resting in the silver sand.

And the old plantation's calling to me, Oh, come, come back,
From the life that's just a-waiting there for you always,
From the trouble, and the bustle, and the agitating hum
That the city keeps going on all the day.

I'm tired of the city; take me back to Sandy Side,
Where the honest ones can live and play and eat.
Where we draw a simple living from the forest and the tide,
And the days are fair, and every night is sweet.
'Cause the old plantation's calling to me, Oh, come, come back.
And the Chesapeake is saying, "That's the thing,"
While my little cabin beckons, though its mouth is closed and dumb,
I'm coming, and my heart begins to sing.

sae_mgt_text:
Go away and quit that noise, Miss Lucy,
Put that music book away;
What's the use to keep on trying?
If you practice till you're gray,
You can't start no notes a-flying
Like the ones that pants and rings
From the kitchen to the big woods
When Malindy sings.

You haven't got the organs full
To make the sound come right,
You haven't got the turns and twists
To make it sweet and light.
Tell you one thing now, Miss Lucy,
And I'm telling you for true:
When it comes to really right singing,
It ain't no easy thing to do.

Easy enough for folks to holler,
Looking at the lines and dots,
When there's nobody to sense it,
And the tune comes in in spots;
But for real melodious music
That just strikes your heart and clings,
Just you stand and listen with me
When Malindy sings.

Ain't you never heard Malindy?
Blessed soul, take up the cross!
Look here, ain't you joking, honey?
Well, you don't know what you lose.
You ought to hear that gal a-wailing,
Robins, larks, and all them things,
Heave their mouths and hide their faces
When Malindy sings.

The fiddling man just stop his fiddling,
Lay his fiddle on the shelf;
Mocking-bird quit trying to whistle,
'Cause he's just so shame of himself.
Folks playing on the banjo
Drop their fingers on the strings--
Bless your soul--forgot to move 'em
When Malindy sings.

She just spreads her mouth and yells,
"Come to Jesus," till you hear
Sinners' trembling steps and voices,
Timid, like a-drawin' near;
Then she turns to "Rock of Ages,"
Simply to the cross she clings,
And you find your tears a-drooping
When Malindy sings.

Who said that humble praises
With the Master never counts?
Hush your mouth, I hear that music,
As it rises up and mounts--
Floating by the hills and valleys,
Way above this burying sod,
As it makes its way in glory
To the very gates of God!

Oh, it's sweeter than the music
Of an educated band;
And it's dearer than the battle's
Song of triumph in the land.
It seems holier than evening
When the solemn church bell rings,
As I sit and calmly listen
While Malindy sings.

Tiousaw, stop that barking, hear me!
Mandy, make that child keep still;
Don't you hear the echoes calling
From the valley to the hill?
Let me listen, I can hear it,
Through the breath of angels' wings,
Soft and sweet, "Swing Low, Sweet Chariot,"
As Malindy sings.

sae_mgt_text:
To R. V.P.

Come, listen while your uncle sings,
About how low the sweet chariot swings—
The truant angel, without wings,
My little touzé head.

Stop! Stop! How dare you laugh at me,
Because I have spoiled the time and key;
Do you think I am Black Patty,
My little touzé head?

Oh, honey lamb! Those sparkling eyes,
That often laugh and seldom cries,
Are surely a gift given by nature,
My little touzé head.

And those wee hands so soft and sweet
Mingle with those toddling, velvet feet,
Just to round you out, complete,
My little touzé head.

Smart! You are smart as smart can be,
Knowing your every A, B, C,
Plum on down to X, Y, Z,
My little touzé head.

The man does not know much he misses,
If he ain't got no niece like this;
From your uncle one more kiss,
My little touzé head!

I wish some magic would allow it,
(By charm or craft—doesn't matter how)
That you stay just as you are, right now,
My little touzé head.

sae_mgt_text:
There's a sort of threatening feeling in the blowing of the breeze,
    And I'm feeling kind of squeamish in the night;
  I'm walking around, looking at the different style of trees,
    And measuring their thickness and their height.
  For there's something mighty suspicious in the looks the crows give,
    As they pass me and my family on the ground,
  So it occurs to me that likely, if I care to try and live,
    It concerns me for to commence to look around.

  There's a curious kind of shiver running up and down my back,
    And I feel my feathers ruffling all the day,
  And my legs commence to tremble every blessed step I make;
    When I see an ax, I turn my head away.
  Folks are going to me with goodies, and they're treating me with care,
    And I'm fat in spite of all that I can do.
  I'm mistrustful of the kindness that's around me everywhere,
    For it's just too good, and frequent, to be true.

  Snow's a-falling on the meadows, all around me now is white,
    But I'm still kept on a-roosting on the fence;
  Isham comes and feels my breastbone, and he hefted me last night,
    And he's gone around a-grinning ever since.
  'T ain't the snow that makes me shiver; 't ain't the cold that makes me
       shake;
    'T ain't the winter-time itself that's affecting me;
  But I think the time is coming, and I'd better make a break,
    For to sit with Mister Possum in his tree.

  When you hear the crows singing, and the quail all are gay,
    'T ain't the time for birds like me to be around;
  When the hickory chip is flying, and the log's been carried away,
    Then it's dangerous to be roosting nigh the ground.

  Grin on, Isham! Sing on, crows! But I flop my wings and go
    For the shelter of the very highest tree,
  For there's too much close attention--and there's too much falling snow--
    And it's too near Christmas morning now for me.

sae_mgt_text:
But how dear a dollar
      Is a mighty friend,
    In the dead of winter,
      If you're idle then.
    Winds may be howling,
      Whizzing through the trees!
    Needn't worry, darky,
      You're not going to freeze!

    Summer is flying,
      Breezes getting cool!
    Better be laying
      In your winter fuel!
    Leaves begin to falling,
      Harvesting is done,
    Birds are now trooping
      Southward with the sun.

    Hoeing time is over,
      Darky take your rest!
    Throw off working harness,
      Don your Sunday best!
    Fiddles and the banjos—
      Get them all in tune,
    Manipulate the ditties
      That give the soul a boon!

    In the spring and summer,
      Darky what have you done?
    Riding on the excursions,
      Having lots of fun?
    Dancing with the ladies,
      Spending all you've got?
    Thinking because it's summer,
      It will always be hot?

    You're the kind that comes
      Knocking on the cabin door,
    For to get assistance,
      Tell her tale of woe.
    Then's the time to show you
      We're not an easy thing,
    Providing for your stomachs
      With a hoe earning.

    What you need is a lesson
      In the experience school.
    Get the realization
      Where you've been a fool.
    Then you'll get the idea,
      Dollar is your friend,
    Learn to be more careful
      How you spend your money.

sae_mgt_text:
They had a great big party down at Tom's the other night;
  Was I there? You bet! I never in my life saw such a sight;
  All the folks from four plantations were invited, and they came,
  They came trooping thick as children when they hear a fife and drum.
  Everybody dressed their finest--Heel your mouth and get away,
  Ain't seen such fancy dressing since last quarterly meeting day;
  Girls all dressed in silks and satins, not a wrinkle nor a crease,
  Eyes a-batting, teeth a-shining, hair brushed back as slick as grease;
  Skirts all tucked and puffed and ruffled, every blessed seam and stitch;
  If you'd seen them with their mistresses, couldn't swear to which was which.

It was Christmas Eve, I recall it was a mighty gloomy day—
Both the weather and the people—not a one of us was gay;
You'll think that's mighty funny 'til I try to make it clear,
For a darky's always happy when the holidays are near.

But we weren't, for that morning Master had told us we must go,
He'd been paying us since freedom, but he couldn't pay no more;
He was never used to planning before he got so poor and old,
So he's going to give up trying, and the homestead must be sold.

I can see him standing now upon the step as clear as day,
With the wind a-kind of fondling through his hair all thin and gray;
And I remember how he trembled when he said, "It's hard for me,
Not to make your Christmas brighter, but I vow it wasn't to be."

All the women were a-crying, and the men, too, on the sly,
And I noticed something shining even in old Master's eye.
But we all stood still to listen as old Ben came from the crowd
And spoke up, a-trying to steady down his voice and make it loud:—

"Look here, Master, I've been serving you for lo! these many years,
And now, since we've got freedom and you're kind of poor, it appears
That you want us all to leave you 'cause you don't think you can pay.
If my memory hasn't fooled me, seems that what I heard you say.

"In other words, you wants us to forget that you've been kind,
And as soon as you are helpless, we're to leave you here behind.
Well, if that's the way this freedom acts on people, white or black,
You can just tell Mister Lincoln for to take his freedom back.

"We're going to work this old plantation for whatever we can get,
For I know it did support us, and the place can do it yet.
Now the land is yours, the hands are ours, and I reckon we'll be brave,

It seems that people are mighty curious
    In the way they think and act.
  They just spend their days a-mixing
    Up the things in almanacs.
  Now, I mind my next door neighbor,--
    He's a mighty likely man,
  But he never thinks of nothing
    Except just to plot and plan.

  All the winter he was planning
    How he'd get his sassafras
  Just as soon as ever Springtime
    Put some greenness in the grass.
  And he allowed a little sooner
    He could stand a cooler breeze
  So's to make a little money
    From the sugar-water trees.

  In the summer, he'd be worrying
    Out the lining of his soul,
  Trying to calculate and fashion
    How he'd get his winter coal;
  And I believe he got his judgment
    Just so tuckered out and thinned
  That he thought a robin's whistle
    Was the whistle of the wind.

  Why won't folks give up their planning,
    And just be content to know
  That they're getting all that's for them
    In the days that come and go?
  Why won't folks quit moving forward?
    Ain't it better just to stand
  And be satisfied with living
   In the season that's at hand?

  It's enough for me to listen
    When the birds are singing around,
  Without a-guessing what'll happen
    When the snow is on the ground.
  In the Springtime and the summer,
    I lay sorrow on the shelf;
  And I know old Mister Winter
    Going to hustle for himself.

  We have been put here for a purpose,
    But the question that has risen
  And made lots of people differ
    Is just what that purpose is.
  Now, according to my reasoning,
    Here's the point where I've arrived,
  Since the Lord put life into us,
    We were put here for to live!

Eight of them here, all told, and yet
These eyes of mine are writing wet;
My heart is aching hard, and so,
The way it never ached before;
My soul is pleading, "Lord, give back
This little lonesome baby, black,
This one, this last poor helpless one
Whose little race was too soon run."

Poor Little Jim, just four years old,
Lying down so still and cold.
Somehow it doesn't seem hardly fair,
To have my baby lying there
Without a smile upon his face,
Without a look about the place;
He used to be so full of fun
It doesn't seem right that all's done.

There are eight in all, but I don't care,
There wasn't a single one to spare;
The world was big, so was my heart,
And this here baby owned its part;
The house was poor, their clothes were rough,
But there was meat and meal enough;
And there was room for little Jim;
Oh, Lord, what made you call for him?

It does seem monstrous hard today,
To lay this baby boy away;
I'd learned to love his teasing smile,
He might have been left awhile;
You wouldn't have thought with all the folks,
That's around here mixing tears and jokes,
The Lord would have had the time to see
This child and take him away from me.

But let it go, I reckon Jim,
Will just go right straight up to Him
That took him from his mammy's nest
And left this aching in my breast,
And looking in that father's face
And remembering this lone sorrowful place,
He'll say, "Good Lord, you ought to have
Done something to comfort dad."

A woman's a curious creature, and there is no doubting that.
She's a mass of funny capers from her slippers to her hat.
If you try to understand her, and you fail, just up and say:
"There isn't a bit of use to try to understand a woman's way."

I don't mean to be complaining, but I'm just setting down
Some of my own observations, when I cast my eye around.
If you ask me to prove it, I can do it mighty fine,
For there is no better example than this very wife of mine.

In the very heart of midnight, when I'm sleeping good and sound,
I can hear a sort of rustling and somebody moving 'round.
And I say, "Lize, what you doing?" But she frowns and shakes her head,
"Hush your mouth, I'm only turning of the children in the bed.

"Don't you know a child gets restless, lying all the night one way?
And you've got to kind of arrange him several times before the day?
So the little necks won't worry, and the little backs won't break;
Don't you think because children are children they haven't got pain and ache."

So she shakes them, and she twists them, and she turns them all about,
'Til I don't see how the children ever keeps from hollering out.
Then she lifts them head downwards, so they won't get liver-grown,
But they snooze just as peaceful as a lizard on a stone.

When it's almost time for waking on the dawn of Judgment Day,
Seems like I can hear old Gabriel lay his trumpet down and say,
"Who is that walking 'round so easy, down on earth among the dead?"--
It will be Lizy up a-turning of the children in the bed.

The wind is blowing warm,  
And it comes from the bay;  
There is a kind of mist arising  
All along the muddy way.  
There is no sign of frost  
On the ground or in the sky,  
And it is useless to hope  
That the snow will begin to fly.  
It is going to be a green Christmas,  
And sad indeed the day for me.  
I wish this was the last one  
That I would ever see.  

They are dancing in the cabin,  
They are sparkling by the tree;  
But dancing times and sparkling  
Are all passed by for me.  
They are feasting in the big house,  
With all the windows wide—  
Is that the way for people  
To meet the Christmas tide?  
It is going to be a green Christmas,  
No matter what you say.  
It is we who will remember  
And grieve to come the day.  

There is only a brief of dampness  
Clinging to my cheek;  
The air has been dark and heavy  
And threatening for a week,  
But without signs of winter,  
Though winter seems so dear—  
The winter is out of season,  
And Christmas Eve is here.  
It is going to be a green Christmas,  
And oh, how sad the day!  
Go ask the hungry churchwarden,  
And see what he will say.  

They are Allen on the hillside,  
And Marfy in the plain;  
For Christmas was like springtime,  
And came with sun and rain.  
There are Callie, John, and Susie,  
With only this one left;  
And now the curse is coming  
With murder in his breath.  
It is going to be a green Christmas—  
Just hear my words and see:  
Before the summer beckons  
They many will weep with me.

They had been speaking in the courthouse,
And laws aplenty too,
It was the finest kind of show
I'd ever seen before.
Of course, I had to be there
In the middle of the crowd,
And I cheered with the others
When the speaker rose and bowed.

I was kind of disappointed
At the smallness of the man,
Since I'd always pictured great folks
On a more expansive plan;
But I thought I could respect him
And take in the words he said,
For there surely was something knowing
In the bald spot on his head.

But it did seem sort of funny
After waiting for a week
That the people kept on shouting
So the man just couldn't speak;
The horns they blared a little,
Then they let loose on the drums—
Someone told me they were playing
"See the conquering hero comes."

"Well," said I, "you all are white folks,
But you're surely acting queer.
What's the use of heroes coming
If they can't talk when they're here?"
After while they let him open,
And that man he waded in,
And he fought the wars all over,
Winning victories like sin.

When he came down to the present,
Then he made the feathers fly.
He just waded in on money,
And he played the tariff high.
And he said the colored question;
It was over, solved, and done,
That the colored was his brother,
Every blessed mother's son.

Well, he settled all the trouble
That had been pestering the land,
Then he sat down amid the cheering
And the playing of the band.
I was feeling mighty happy
'Til I heard somebody speak,
"Well, that's his side of the business,
But you wait for Jones next week."

They were talking in the cabin; they were talking in the hall;
But I listened kind of careless, not thinking 'bout it all.
And on Sunday, too, I noticed, they were whispering mightily much,
Standing all around the roadside when they let us out of church.
But I didn't think 'bout it 'till the middle of the week,
And my Elias came to see me, and somehow he couldn't speak.
Then I saw all in a minute what he'd come to see me for;
They had enlisted colored soldiers and my Elias was going to war.

Oh, I hugged him, and I kissed him, and I begged him not to go;
But he told me that his conscience, it was calling to him so,
And he couldn't bear to linger when he had a chance to fight
For the freedom they had given him and the glory of the right.
So he kissed me, and he left me, when I'd promised to be true;
And they put a knapsack on him, and a coat all colored blue.
So I gave him Papa's old Bible from the bottom of the drawer,
When they enlisted colored soldiers and my Elias went to war.

But I thought of all the weary miles that he would have to tramp,
And I couldn't be contented when they took him to the camp.
Why my heart nigh broke with grieving 'till I saw him on the street;
Then I felt like I could go and throw my body at his feet.
For his buttons were a-shining, and his face was shining, too,
And he looked so strong and mighty in his coat of soldier blue,
That I called out, "Step up, man," though my throat was sore and raw,
When they enlisted colored soldiers and my Elias went to war.

Old Mistress cried when Master left her; young Miss mourned her brother Ned;
And I didn't know their feelings were the very words they said
When I told them I was sorry. They had done given up their all;
But they seemed only more proud that their men had heeded the call.
Both my masters went in gray suits, and I loved the Yankee blue,
But I thought that I could sorrow for the losing of them too;
But I couldn't, for I didn't know half of what I saw,
'Till they enlisted colored soldiers and my Elias went to war.

Master Jack came home all sickly; he was broke for life, they said;
And they left my poor young master somewhere on the roadside—dead.
When the women cried and mourned them, I could feel it through and through,
For I had a loved one fighting in the way of danger, too.
Then they told me they had laid him somewhere way down south to rest,
With the flag that he had fought for shining dark across his breast.
Well, I cried, but then I reckon that's what God had called him for,
When they enlisted colored soldiers and my Elias went to war.

  When the thoughts they keep on dropping
    Were not big enough to find?

  But the first name hits me better,
    Because they never touch a drought.

  Who do not set their words so skimpy

There is snow upon the meadows, there is snow upon the hill,
  And the little branches' waters are all glistening and still;
  The wind goes round the cabin like a spirit wandering around,
  And the children shakes and shivers as they listen to the sound.
  There is hickory in the fireplace, where the blaze is rising high,
  But the heat it makes ain't warming up the gray clouds in the sky.
  Now and then I just peek outside, then I hurry to the door,
  Lord have mercy on my body, how I wish it wouldn't snow!

  I can stand the hottest summer, I can stand the wettest fall,
  I can stand the chilly springtime in the ploughland, but that's all;
  For the very hottest fire never tells my skin a thing,
  When the snow commences a-flying, and the wind begins to sing.
  There is plenty wood around us, and I chop and tote it in,
  But the thoughts that I'm a-thinking while I'm working is a sin.
  I can keep from downright sweating all the time I'm on the go,
  But my heart is full of curses when I'm tramping through the snow.

  What do you say, you Lishy Davis, that you see a possum's tracks?
  Look here, boy, you stop your fooling, bring old Spot, and bring the ax.
  Am I cold? Go away, now, Mandy, what you think I'm made of?--show,
  Why this wind is just as gentle, and this ain't no kind of snow.
  This here weather's just as healthy as the warmest summer days.
  All you children step up lively, pile on wood and keep a blaze.
  What's the use of getting scared because there's snow upon the ground?
  Huh-uh, I'm a regular snowbird if there's any possum around.

  Go on, Spot, don't be so foolish; don't you see the signs of feet.
  What you howling for? Keep still, sir, for the cold is pretty sweet;
  But we're going out on business, and it's business of the kind
  That must put a dog and donkey in a happy frame of mind.
  Yes, you're cold; I know it, Spotty, but you just stay close to me,
  And I'll make you hot as cotton when we strike the happy tree.
  No, I don't like winter weather, and I'd wish 'twas always June,
  If it wasn't for the tracking of the possum and the coon.

These eating folks may tell me of the glories of spring lamb,
And the toothsome delights of turkey eaten with celery and with jam;
Of beefsteak fried with onions, and seasoned up so fine--
But you just give me hog-meat, and I'm happy all the time.

When the frost is on the pumpkin and the snowflakes fill the air,
I then begin rejoicing--hog-killing time is near;
And the visions of the future then fill my nightly dreams,
For the time is fast approaching for the delicious pork and beans.

We folks that are from the country may be behind the sun--
We don't like city eatings, with beefsteaks that aren't done--
Though mutton chops are splendid, and those veal cutlets fine,
To me it's not like a spare-rib, or great big chunk of chine.

Just talk to me about hog-meat, if you want to see me pleased,
For boiled with beans it's glorious, or made in hog-head cheese;
And I could just be happy, without money, clothes or house,
With plenty years and pig feet made in old-fashioned "souse."

I confess I'm only human, I have my joys and cares--
Some days the clouds hang heavy, some days the skies are fair;
But I forgive my enemies, my heart is free from hate,
When my bread is filled with cracklins and there's chitlins on my plate.

Though possum meat is glorious with potatoes in the pan,
But put alongside pork sausage it takes a backward stand;
Of all your fancy eatings, just give to me for mine
Some souse or pork or chitlins, some spare-rib, or the chine.

    Looking mighty pleased and glad.

  Samuel smiling and a-singing

Has no more enchanting spot.

Seems to go all around to roam.

And you begin to feel a tickling in your toe and in your heel;
If you think you have religion and you want to keep it, too,
You just better take a hint and get yourself clean out of view.
For the time is mighty tempting when the tune is in the swing,
For a darky, saint or sinner man, to cut the pigeon-wing.
And you couldn't help from dancing if your feet were bound with twine,
When Angelina Johnson comes a-swinging down the line.

Don't you know Miss Angelina? She's the darling of the place.
Why, there ain't no high-toned lady with such manners and such grace.
She can move across the cabin, with its planks all rough and worn;
Just the same as if she was dancing on old mistress' ballroom floor.
In fact, you don't see no cabin--everything you see looks grand,
And that one old squeaky fiddle sounds to you just like a band;
Cotton britches look like broadcloth and a linsey dress look fine,
When Angelina Johnson comes a-swinging down the line.

Some folks say that dancing's sinful, and the blessed Lord, they say,
Is going to punish us for stepping when we hear the music play.
But I tell you I don't believe it, for the Lord is wise and good,
And He made the banjo's metal and He made the fiddle's wood,
And He made the music in them, so I don't quite think He'll care
If our feet keep time a little to the melodies we hear.
Why, there's something downright holy in the way our faces shine,
When Angelina Johnson comes a-swinging down the line.

And the young men, they're saying, "I'm going to make that damsel mine,"
When Angelina Johnson comes a-swinging down the line.

sae_mgt_text:
In the dead of night I sometimes
    Get to thinking of the past
  And the days when slavery held me
    In my misery—hard and fast.
  Though the time was mighty trying,
    In these hours somehow it seems
  That a brighter light comes slipping
    Through the coverings of my dreams.

  And my mind forgets the whippings,
    Drops the fear of block and lash
  And flies straight to something joyful
    In a second’s lightning flash.
  Then it seems I see a vision
    Of a dearer long ago,
  Of the children tumbling round me
    By my rough old cabin door.

  Talk about your gorgeous mansions
    And your big house great and grand,
  Just bring up the finest palace
    That you know in all the land.
  But there’s something dearer to me,
    Something fairer to my eyes
  In that cabin, less you bring me
    To your mansion in the skies.

  I can see the light a-shining
    Through the chinks between the logs,
  I can hear the way-off baying
    Of my master’s hunting dogs,
  And the neighing of the horses
    Stamping on the old barn floor,
  But above these sounds the laughing
    At my dear old cabin door.

  We would gather there at evening,
    All my friends would come around,
  And it wasn’t any time till, bless you,
    You could hear the banjo’s sound.
  You could see the darkies dancing
    Pigeon wing and heel and toe—
  Joyous times, I tell you people,
    Round that same old cabin door.

  But at times my thoughts get sadder,
    As I recollect the folks,
  And their frolicking and talking
    With their laughing and their jokes.
  And it hurts me when I remember
    That I’ll never see no more
  Them dear faces gathered smiling
    Round that poor old cabin door.

sae_mgt_text:
Dear Miss Lucy, I've been thinking that I'd write to you long ago,
But writing's a tedious task, and you know just how it is.
But I've got some leisure time, so I take my pen in hand
To let you know my feelings since I reached this foreign land.

I'm quite well, I'm glad to tell you, though the climate's not to blame,
And I hope that when these lines reach you, they'll find you in good frame.
For I'm feeling rather homesick - that's as natural as can be,
When a fellow's more than three thousand miles across that awful sea.

Don't let anyone fool you about the ocean being grand;
If you want to see the billows, you just view them from the land.
As for the people, we thought that all white folks were alike;
But these Englishmen are different, and they're curious, for a fact.

First, they're heavier and redder in their makeup and their looks,
And they don't put salt or pepper in a blessed thing they cook!
When they give you good old turnips, carrots, parsnips, beets, and such,
If there's no one to tell you, you can't distinguish which is which.
When I thought I was eating chicken - you may believe this to be a lie -
But the waiter convinced me that I was eating rabbit pie.
And they'd think that you were crazy - just a regular raving lunatic -
If you'd speak about a possum or a piece of good old raccoon.

Oh, it's mighty nice, this traveling, and I'm kind of glad I came.
But I reckon now I'm willing to take my way back home.
I've seen the Crystal Palace, and I've heard their string-band play,
But I haven't seen any banjos laying around this way.
Just give old Jim Bowles a banjo, and he wouldn't go very far,
Before he'd outplayed all these fiddlers, with their flourish and their stir.

Everyone I've met has been monstrous kind and good;
But I think I'd like it better to be down in Jones's wood,
Where we used to have such frolics, Lucy, you and me and Nelse,
Though my appetite would call me, if there wasn't anything else.
I'd just like to have some sweet potatoes roasted in the skin;
I'm longing for my chitlins and my mustard greens again;
I'm wishing for some buttermilk, and cornbread, good and brown,
And a drop of good old bourbon to wash my feelings down!

And I'm coming back to see you just as early as I can,
So you better not go sparking with that worthless scoundrel Quin!
Well, I reckon I must close now; write as soon as this reaches you;
Give my love to Sister Mandy and to Uncle Isham, too.
Tell the folks I send them howdy; give a kiss to pap and mam;
Closing, I am, dear Miss Lucy, Still Your Own True-Loving Sam.

P.S. If you can't make out this letter, lay it by or put it on the shelf,
And when I get home, I'll read it, darling, to you myself.

    For to scrape up a dollar

And you think you’ll fall to the wall,
Salt and pepper never will save you
From an ever-lasting fall.

You’ll keep always looking up,
Remembering some the world’s best jewels
Drank from this same bitter cup!

And no place to lay your head,
And the meadows and the corn fields
Are the only place for your bed;

Before you, putting on their airs,
With their silks and with their satins,
And all other kinds of wares.

If you’ve got the right stuff in you,
You’ll keep always looking up,
Remembering some the world’s best jewels
Drank from this same bitter cup!

As they pass you in their scorn;

Because they think that you are down.

    And the chips have been falling fast and thick;
They have cut the biggest hickory that the mules can tote away,
    And they've laid it down and soaked it in the creek.
Then they took it to the big house and they piled the wood around
    In the fireplace from ash floor to the flue,
While old Ezry starts the hymn that every year has got to sound
    When the back-log first commences burning through.

Old Master is smiling on the daisies from the hall,
Old Mistress is standing in the door,
And the young folks, males and misses, are trying, one and all,
    For to make us feel it's Christmas time for sure.
And our hearts are full of pleasure, for we know the time is ours
    For to dance or do just what we want to do.
And there ain't no overseer and no other kind of powers
    That can stop us while that log is burning through.

They're a-working in the quarters preparing for the feast,
    So the little pigs are feeling kind of shy.
The chickens ain't so trustful as they were, to say the least,
    And the wise old hens are roosting mighty high.
You couldn't get a gobbler to look you in the face--
    I ain't saying what the turkey's prospects are true;
But it's mighty dangerous traveling for the critters on the place
    From the time that log commences burning through.

    And, bless me, that's the tooting of a horn!

    Keep your mind upon the tune and step it true.
Oh, there ain't no time for stopping and there ain't no time for rest,
    For it's Christmas and the back-log's burning through!

The Young Master Asks for a Story

What did you say, my child?
You are enough to drive me wild.
You want a story; just hear that!
Where will I find a story at?
Didn't I tell you three last night?
Go away, honey, you're not right.
I have something else to do,
Besides just telling tales to you.
Tell you just one? Let me see
What that one is going to be.
When you're old, your memory fails;
It seems like I don't know any tales.
Well, sit down there in that chair,
Keep still if you want to hear.
Take that chin up off your hands,
Sit up nice now. Goodness lands!
Hold yourself up like your father.
Bet nobody ever saw
Him scrunched down like you were then--
High-tone boys make high-tone men.

Once there was an old black bear,
Used to live around here somewhere,
In a cave. He was so big
He could carry off a pig
Like you pick up a chicken,
Or your little bit of a pup.
And he had two great big eyes,
Just about a saucer's size.
Why, they looked like balls of fire
Jumping around upon a wire
When that bear was mad; and laws!
But you ought to have seen his paws!
Did I see them? How you expect
I'm going to recall
This here yarn I'm trying to spin
If you keep on putting in?
You keep still and don't you chirp
Less I'll send you off to sleep.
This here bear would go tromping around,
Eating everything he found;
No one couldn't have a farm
But that bear would do them harm;
And they couldn't catch the scamp.
Anywhere he wanted to tramp.
There the scoundrel would make his track,
Do his duty and come on back.
He was such a sly old limb,
Traps were just like fun to him.

Now, down near where Mister Bear
Lived, there was a weasel there;
But they weren't friends at all,
Because the weasel was so small.
And the bear would, just for sass,
Turn his nose up when he'd pass.
Weasels are small, of course, but my!
Those are animals that are sly.
So this here one says, says he,
"I'll just fix that bear, you see."
So he fixes up his plan
And hunts up the farmer.
When the farmer sees him come,
He commences looking mighty glum,
And he catches up a stick;
But the weasel speaks up quick:
"Hold on, Mister Farmer man,
I want to explain a little plan.
If you wait, I'll tell you where
And just how to catch old Bear.
But I tell you now you must
Give me one fat chicken first."
Then the man he scratches his head,
Last he says, "I'll make the trade."
So the weasel eats his hen,
Smacks his mouth and says, "Well, then,
Set your trap and bait tonight,
And I'll catch the bear all right."
Then he ups and goes to see
Mister Bear, and says, says he:
"Well, friend Bear, we ain't been friends,
But tonight I'd feel like being so.
If you ain't too proud to steal,
We can get a splendid meal.
Of course I wouldn't come to you,
But it must be done by two;
It's a trap, but we can beat
All their tricks and get the meat."
"Of course I'm with you," says the bear,
"Come on, weasel, show me where."
Well, they trot along until
That air meat begins to smell
In the trap. Then weasel says:
"Now you put your paw this way
While I hold the spring back so,
Then you grab the meat and go."
Well, the bear he had to grin
As he put his big paw in,
Then he juked up, but--kerbing!
Weasel done let go the spring.
"There now," says the weasel, "there,
I have caught you, Mister Bear!"
Oh, that bear did snort and spout,
Trying his best to get out,
But the weasel says, "Goodbye!
Weasel small, but weasel sly."
Then he turned his back and ran
Told the farmer what he done.
So the farmer comes down there,
With an axe and kills the bear.

There now, ain't that story fine?
Run along now, never mind.
Want some more, you rascal, you?
No, sir! no, sir! that'll do.

    Makes you over good and new,

    Seems to me it's summer time,

    I'm a feeling just that prime--
    And her name is Delia.

This here love's a curious thing,
    Changes 'round the season,
    Makes you sad or makes you sing,
    Without no earthly reason.
    Sometimes I go moping round,
    Then again I'm leaping;
    Spirits always up and down
    Even when I'm sleeping.

    And they keep me pitching,
    Like the apple dumplings when

    Catching Delia by the arm
    So's to take her from me.

    Even when I'm dreaming.

    So's you leave me Delia.

sae_mgt_text:
The times are mighty stirring among the people up our way,
They disputing and they arguing and fussing night and day;
And all this monstrous trouble that it makes me tired to tell
Is about that Lucy Jackson that was such a mighty belle.

She was the preacher's favored, and he told the church one night
That she traveled through the cloud of sin a-bearing of a light;
But, now, I allow he's thinking that she must have lost her lamp,
'Cause Lucy's done backslid and there's trouble in the camp.

Her daddy wants to beat her, but her mama dares him to,
For she's looking at the question from a woman's point of view;
And she says that now she wouldn't have it different if she could;
That her daughter only acted just like any other would.

'Course you know when women argue, they are mighty easy led
By their hearts and don't go fooling about the reasons of the head.
So her mama laid the law down (she ain't recognizing wrong),
But you got to make allowance for the cause that goes along.

Now the cause that made Miss Lucy for to throw her grace away
I'm afraid won't bear inspection when it comes to Judgment Day;
Though the same thing's been a-working ever since the world began,—
The woman disobeying for to entice along a man.

If you attended the revivals which we held the winter past,
You can recollect that converts were a-coming thick and fast;
But there ain't no use in talking, they were all left in the lurch
When old Mrs. Jackson's daughter found her peace and took the church.

Why, she shouted over every inch of Ebenezer's floor;
Up into the preacher's pulpit and from there down to the door;
Then she hugged and squeezed her mama, and she hugged and kissed her dad,
And she struck out at her sister, people said, like she was mad.

I have attended some revivals that were lively in my day,
And I've seen folks get religion in most every kind of way;
But I tell you, and you believe me that I'm speaking true indeed,
That gal took her religion harder than the hardest yet I've seen.

Well, from that, it was "Sister Jackson, won't you please do this or that?"
She must always start the singing when they'd pass around the hat,
And it seemed they wasn't nothing in that church that could go by
Without Sister Lucy Jackson had a finger in the pie.

But the saying's mighty truthful that it's easier to sail
When the sea is calm and gentle than to weather out a gale.
That's what made this woman's trouble; if the storm had kept away,
She'd have had enough religion for to last out her day.

Lucy went with 'Lisha Davis, but when she joined church, you know
There was lots of little places that, of course, she couldn't go;
And she had to give up dancing and her singing and her play.—
Now it's natural that such goings-on would drive a man away.

So, when Lucy got so solemn, Ike he started for to go
With a gal who was a sinner and could make a better show.
Lucy just went on to meeting like she didn't care a rap,
But my experience kept me thinking there was something going to drop.

For a gal won't let religion or no other sort of thing
Stop her when she takes a notion that she wants a wedding ring.
You can promise her the blessings of a happy after life
(And it's nice to be an angel), but she'd rather be a wife.

So when Christmas come and master gave a frolic on the lawn,
Didn't surprise me not the littlest seeing Lucy looking on.
And I saw a warning lightning go a-flashing from her eye
Just as 'Lisha and his new gal went a-gallivanting by.

And that Tildy, umph! she giggled, and she gave her dress a flirt
Like the people she was passing was as common as the dirt;
And the minute she was dancing, why that gal put on more airs
Than a cat a-taking kittens up a pair of winding stairs.

She could afford to show her smartness, for she couldn't help but know
That with just the present dancers she was owner of the floor;
But I think she'd kind of cooled down if she happened on the sly
For to noticed that there lightning that I saw in Lucy's eye.

And she wouldn't been so astonished when the people gave a shout,
And Lucy threw her mantle back and come a-gliding out.
Some arms was there to take her and she fluttered down the floor
Like a feather from a bed-tick when the wind commences to blow.

Soon as Tildy saw the trouble, she just turned and tossed her head,
But seemed like she lost her spirit, all her daringness was dead.
Didn't cut another caper any time the blessed night;
But the other one, it looked like couldn't get enough delight.

When you keeps a colt a-standing in the stable all along,
When he do get out it's natural he'll be pulling mighty strong.
If you will tie up your feelings, here's the best advice to take,
Look out for an awful loosening when the string that holds them breaks.

Lucy's mama groaned to see her, and her pappy stormed and tore,
But she kept right on a-holding to the center of the floor.
So they went and asked the pastor if he couldn't make her quit,
But the telling of the story threw the preacher in a fit.

Tildy Taylor chewed her handkerchief till she'd chewed it in a hole,—
All the sinners was rejoicing 'cause

      Then he stops to fan,
        Along towards night.

  He smells the bacon cooking, and he hears the fire hum;
  And he commences to sing, though working pretty nigh done made him dumb,
        Along towards night.

    With his hoe upon his shoulder
      Then he goes along,
        Along towards night.
    And he keeps time a-stepping
      With a little song,
        Along towards night.
  The resting-time's a-coming, and the time to drink and eat;
  A baby's toddling towards him on its little dusty feet,
  And he's going towards his cabin, and his supper's mighty sweet,
        Along towards night.

    There his Caroline minds the kettle,
      Rufus minds the child,
        Along towards night;
    And the sweat rolls down his forehead,
      Mixing with his smile,
        Along towards night.
  He tosses his piccaninny, and he hums a little tune;
  The working all is over, and the supper coming soon;
  The working time's December, but the resting time is June,
        Along towards night.

    Hits a tender place,
        Along towards night;

  The cabin's like the big house, and the fire's like the sun;
  His wife looks mighty lovely, and the child the prettiest one;
  Why, it's blessed, just a-living when a body's work is done.
        Along towards night.

We are gathered here, my brothers,
    In this howling wilderness,
  For to speak some words of comfort
    To each other in distress.
  And we choose for our subject
    This--we'll explain it by and by;
    "And the Lord said, 'Moses, Moses,'
    And the man said, 'Here am I.'"

  Now old Pharaoh, down in Egypt,
    Was the worst man ever born,
  And he had the Hebrew children
    Down there working in his corn;
  'Twas well the Lord got tired of his fooling,
    And said he: "I'll let him know--
  Look here, Moses, go tell Pharaoh
    For to let those children go."

  "And if he refuse to do it,
    I will make him rue the hour,
  For I'll empty down on Egypt
    All the vials of my power."
  Yes, he did--and Pharaoh's army
    Wasn't worth a half a dime;
  For the Lord will help his children,
    You can trust him every time.

  And your enemies may assail you
    In the back and in the front;
  But the Lord is all around you,
    For to bear the battle's brunt.
  They can forge your chains and shackles
    From the mountains to the sea;
  But the Lord will send some Moses
    For to set his children free.

  And the land shall hear his thunder,
    Like a blast from Gabriel's horn,
  For the Lord of hosts is mighty
    When he girds his armor on.
  But for fear some one mistakes me,
    I will pause right here to say,
  That I'm still a-preaching ancient,
    I ain't talking 'bout to-day.

  But I tell you, fellow Christians,
    Things will happen mighty strange;
  Now, the Lord done this for Israel,
    And his ways don't never change,
  And the love he showed to Israel
    Wasn't all on Israel spent;
  Now don't run and tell your masters
    That I'm preaching discontent.

  'Cause I am not; I'm a-judging
    Bible people by their acts;
  I am a-giving you the Scripture,
    I am a-handling you the facts.
  Because old Pharaoh believed in slavery,
    But the Lord he let him see,
  That the people he put breath in,--
    Every mother's son was free.

  And there are others think like Pharaoh,
    But they call the Scripture liar,
  For the Bible says "a servant
    Is a-worthy of his hire."
  And you can't get round nor through that,
    And you can't get over it,
  For whatever place you get in,
    This here Bible will fit.

  So you see the Lord's intention,
    Ever since the world began,
  Was that His almighty freedom
    Should belong to every man,
  But I think it would be better,
    If I'd pause again to say,
  That I'm talking 'bout our freedom
    In a Biblical way.

  But the Moses is a-coming,
    And he's coming, sure and fast
  We can hear his feet a-tromping,
    We can hear his trumpet blast.
  But I want to warn you people,
    Don't you get too brighty;
  And don't you get to bragging
    'Bout these things, you wait and see.

  But when Moses with his power
    Comes and sets us children free,
  We will praise the gracious Master.
    That has given us liberty;
  And we'll shout our hallelujahs,
    On that mighty reckoning day,
  When we are recognized as citizens--
    Hush! Children, let us pray!

Oh, there's lots of care and trouble
    In this world to swallow down;
  And old Sorrow's pretty lively
    In her way of getting 'round.
  Yet there's times when I forget them,—
    Aches and pains and troubles all,—
  And it's when I take at evening
    My old banjo from the wall.

  'Bout the time that night is falling
    And my daily work is done,
  And above the shady hilltops
    I can see the setting sun;
  When the quiet, restful shadows
    Are beginning just to fall,—
  Then I take the little banjo
    From its place upon the wall.

  Then my family gathers 'round me
    In the fading of the light,
  As I strike the strings to try them
    If they all are tuned aright.
  And it seems we're so nigh heaven
    We can hear the angels sing
  When the music of that banjo
    Sets my cabin all a-ring.

  And my wife and all the others,—
    Male and female, small and big,—
  Even up to gray-haired granny,
    Seem just bound to do a jig;
  'Til I change the style of music,
    Change the movement and the time,
  And the ringing little banjo
    Plays an old heart-feeling hymn.

  And somehow my throat gets choky,
    And a lump keeps trying to rise
  Like it wanted to catch the water
    That was flowing to my eyes;
  And I feel that I could sort of
    Knock the socks clean off of sin
  As I hear my poor old granny
    With her trembling voice join in.

  Then we all throw in our voices
    For to help the tune out too,
  Like a big camp-meeting choir
    Trying to sing a mourner through.
  And our throats let out the music,
    Sweet and solemn, loud and free,
  'Til the rafters of my cabin
    Echo with the melody.

  Oh, the music of the banjo,
    Quick and devilish, solemn, slow,
  Is the greatest joy and solace
    That a weary slave can know!
  So just let me hear it ringing,
    Though the tune be poor and rough,
  It's a pleasure; and the pleasures
    Of this life are few enough.

  Now, the blessed little angels
    Up in heaven, we are told,
  Don't do nothing all their lifetime
    Except play on harps of gold.
  Now I think heaven'd be more homelike
    If we'd hear some music fall
  From a real old-fashioned banjo,
    Like that one upon the wall.

In lonely woods at night,
When the moon is shining bright,
A coon is sitting on a stump,
Playing the banjo, plinking plump!
Softly floats the mournful strain
Across the dewy, grassy plain—
Plinkity! plinkity! plinking plump!
The coon is playing on the stump!

Every wind and every breeze,
Every twig among the trees,
Echoes with the plinking plump!
The coon is playing on the stump!
Plinkity! plinkity! plinking plump!
The coon is playing on the stump!

As the night glides slowly on,
And the moon slips down by dawn,
And the veil drops from the skies,
And the world opens its eyes,
Dies away the plinking plump!
The coon is playing on the stump!
Plinkity! plinkity! plinking plump!
Stops the coon from playing on the stump.

When the snow begins to fall  
And the wind is cold,  
Mammy starts to call,  
Then she starts to scold:  
"Lucius Lishy Brackett,  
Don't you go out doors;  
Button up your jacket,  
Or you'll get quite frozen."

I sit at the window  
Looking at the ground,  
Nothing near me hidden,  
Mammy isn't around.  
I wish she would let me  
Set down in this chair;  
Pshaw, it wouldn't take me  
Long to get some air.

So I jump down nimble  
As a boy can be,  
Though I'm all a-trimble  
Feared someone'll see me.  
But in half a minute  
I fly out the door  
And I'm knee-deep in it,  
That blessed, snowy floor.

Then I hear a patter  
Coming across the floor,  
Then there comes a clatter  
At the cabin door;  
And my Mammy hollers,  
Spoiling all my joy,  
"Come in from that water,  
Don't I see you, boy?"

When the snow is sifting  
Down as soft as meal,  
What's the use of living  
Except you get the feel  
Of the stuff that's falling—  
Round, white, and damp,  
Without someone calling,  
"Come in here, you scamp!"

Summer is the loving time—
    No matter what you say.
  Night is always bright and prime,
    Better than the day.
  Though the day is sweet and good,
    Birds a-singing fine,
  Pines a-smelling in the wood—
    But the night is mine.

  River whispering “how do you do,”
    As it passes by—
  Moon a-looking down at you,
    Winking on the sly.
  Frogs a-croaking from the pond,
    Singing bass they fill,
  And you listen way beyond
    Old man whip-poor-will.

  Hush up, honey, take my hand,
    Make your footsteps light;
  Something kind of holds the land
    On a summer night.
  Something that you never see
    And you never hear,
  But you feel it in the breeze,
    Something near to tears.

  Something near to tears? That’s so;
    But it’s near to smiles.
  And you feel it as you go
    Down the shining miles.
  Take my hand, my little dove;
    Hush and come away—
  Summer is the time for love,
    Night-time beats the day!

sae_mgt_text:
Best of all the Christmas entertainments
That I actually ever see,
Was the one at Lonesome Valley
At the church of Pastor Weed.

All the old folks and the children
Dressed up and paraded out that night,
To the great big Christmas entertainment
To get their Christmas delight.

When they gathered in that chapel,
Brother, they were thick as hops,
When the children saw the candy,
They smacked their mouths and licked their chops.

They were laughing and clapping their hands,
And their jaws just kept a-cracking,
Like the chitterlings in the pans.

And the old folks tell you, honey,
I believe they were the worst.
They were so anxious for their refreshments
They were almost ready to burst.

Pastor Weed with that swallow tail
And vest of his cut low,
Just had all the flouncing sisters
Legging for to be his beau.

Brother Hookey was puzzled;
Felt so big he thought he was king;
Took a ball bat, rapped for order,
Said, let's clear our throats and sing.

Well, he took his pistol meader,
Gave the lining of the hymn,
And they sang the "Weeping Moses"
And they sang it too, by Jim.

At the conclusion of that ditty,
Deacon Jasper put up a prayer,
Threw his head clear to the ceiling
Though he saw the Gates of Heaven.

This ain't true, I'll eat the possum,
Such a prayer you never heard;
Scratched his head and wept and hollered
Till his eyes like blood were red.

Oh, he's moaning and a-toning
And a-kotching of his breath--
Spit a-gun his hands and rubbed them--
Pound the bench from right to left.

Last he included and the sisters
Started to sing plantation tune.
Brother Hookey didn't like it;
Told them they were most too soon.

But the most fun of the evening
Was when giving presents out.
You'd almost cracked your sides with laughing
Till you'd got almost to hold the gout.

On the tree there was a chicken;
Wasn't labeled with a name.
When the darkies heard about it
Every one put up a claim.

Brother Gardenia spied the chicken
Flopping beneath the Christmas tree;
Made a home run with a holler;
"That chicken is for me!"

Well, sir, when he hollered chicken
'Twas the same as hollering fire,
For that chicken was a stamped
In the church and in the choir.

Some of the sisters that had rheumatics
And the aches for years and years,
For that chicken was a scrambling
And a falling of happy cheers.

Pastor Weed he got so excited
That he ran clear out his coat,
Fell again in the stove kerwollup!
But his head and swore by note.

But he jumped up in a jiffy,
Feeling like he was before,
Gave a bound spring for that chicken,
But by Jinks he's almost too slow.

Though he hit his head a stunner,
Didn't even make a dent,
Because he's so much like the devil,
His head was hard as adamant.

All the time the rest was scuffling
And a-kicking right and left,
Got so bunkshus and bumbastic
They could hardly restrain themselves.

Louder! Louder! Got the jangling
More and more they rang their bluff,
Worse than the grabbing for the chicken
Than when they got at it rough.

Some were pulling out their razors
And a-cursing for the show.
All the sisters got to asking,
Lord have mercy, let us out the door.

Finally Brother Moses with a
Kind of peculiar kind of trick,
Caught the poultry, made a beeline,
Cut a regular double quick.

Then some swore they had been conjured,
Others declared they'd been hoo-dooed,
Left the church with swearing vengeance
In the worst kind of mood.

Way up in the tree,
Old Brother Possum sits!
Hey, there, I see you,
Brother Possum, hiding in the blossom!

You need not act so timid,
Nor act so shy,
There's better, closer friendship
For any possum, close at hand!

Hey, there, Brother Possum,
You're acting mighty contrary;
Just saunter down a minute!
Now, you needn't have no worry,
Nor puzzling thoughts at all!
Come down, you needn't bother
What the barking dogs are up to!

Look here, Brother Possum,
How do you feel kind of scared?
Getting tired of coaxing,
Makes me feel a little dreary!
I don't like so much begging,
Nor I don't like so much pleading,
Especially to my friend,
When there's not a bit of needin'.

Hey, there, Brother Possum,
You're just like old Brother Satan!
Thinking the odds are against you,
And you keep a fellow waiting.
Well, it doesn't matter,
If you insist on me climbing up,
Just hold your breath a minute!
Because right after comes up
Brother Highmen!

Having the ache and pain depart.
I lost that cancerous roomerism,
No more hobbling with that cane.

Things look like the Eden Garden,
Hardly believe this is myself.
This is bliss in every moment,
Tickling my old soul to deft.

That snake oil surely did the business;
Leave those herbs and roots behind.
Bless the Lord! Umph! Gracious Master!
Hardly staying in my old boots!

Go away, children, let your daddy
Have the place all to himself.
For the old man is joyifying
And he is drawing brand new breath.

This old frame is no more shaky;
I'm not most eighty-eight.
Those old joints are just as supple
When I am in my youthful state.

Once more to dance the buck and wing.
Is there among your doubting Thomases
Who think I cannot do that thing?

Oh, I used to cut it, children,
When old fiddling Pete was around.
Had all of the white and black folks
Beat who lived about the town.

And you bet he was a fiddler
To make you dance yourself leg bowl.
Played the sweetest kind of ditties
That just rejoiced your very soul.

Make out me a dancing coon.

Using children in his business;
That is the way he takes to win.

To dance at its old sound.

Git me dancing, lose my leggun
On the last day to lose my crown.

Guess I better get the Bible,
Read the Master's blessed Word.
Leave these here mischievous rascals,
For they are some of the devil's herd.

The grubbing hoe's rusting in the corner,
    And the plow's tumbling down in the field,
  While the whippoorwill's wailing like a mourner
    When his stubborn heart is trying hard to yield.

  In the furrows where the corn was always waving,
    Now the weeds are growing green and rank and tall;
  And the swallows round the whole place are braving
    Like they thought their folks had always owned it all.

  And the big house stands all quiet, dark, and solemn,
    Not a blessed soul in parlor, porch, or lawn;
  Not a guest, nor not a carriage left to haul them,
    For the ones that turned the latch-string out are gone.

  And the banjo's voice is silent in the quarters,
    There isn't a hymn nor corn-song ringing in the air;
  But the murmur of a branch's passing waters
    Is the only sound that breaks the stillness there.

  Where are the darkies, those who used to be dancing
    Every night before the old cabin door?
  Where are the children, those who used to be prancing
    Or a-rolling in the sand or on the floor?

  Where are old Uncle Mordecai and Uncle Aaron?
    Where are Aunt Doshy, Sam, and Kit, and all the rest?

Umph! How some foolish folks want to be white.  
Because they are black, they do not seem quite right.  
They are ashamed of their color; they are ashamed of their race;  
That is why they would like to be white for everyone's sake.  

Because they cannot bleach out, oh, how they deplore  
To be black and deal with such a boring bore.  
To think God sent them all into this land  
With hair that is kinky and faces that are tan.  

First to the left and then next to the right,  
They look to see if there is something in sight  
To make them bleach white and give them cheeks of the rose  
And something to give them a high Roman nose.  

They are kicking and fussing and raising turmoil  
Because they cannot get hold of the right kind of oil  
To take away the kinky effect they cannot bear,  
And make it just like the white folk's aubond hair.  

They use mutton suet and tallow, and lard,  
Oh Lord of Mischief! but don't they try hard!  
To make it look wavy and glossy and slick.  
Then part in the middle, they are right to the quick.  
If they have no hope, why they go get a wig.  
It must be made from white folks' hair, too, by jig.

To wash a wig made from a coon's nappy hair.  

What's the use of kicking  
Because of such rot?  
Because you cannot bleach,  
And turn white on the spot!  

If your hair is kinky,  
You are black as tar,  
Thank the good Lord  
That you are just as you are.

When I come in from the cornfield after working hard all day,
It's amazingly nice to find my supper all on the way;
And it's nice to smell the coffee bubbling over in the pot,
And it's fine to see the meat a-sizzling, teasing-like, and hot.

But when supper time is over, and the things are cleared away,
Then the happy hours that follow are the sweetest of the day.
When my tobacco pipe is started, and the smoke is drawing prime,
My old woman says, "I reckon, Ike, it's candlelighting time."

Then the children snuggle up to me, and all commence to call,
"Oh, say, Daddy, now it's time to make the shadows on the wall."
So I put my hands together—every daddy knows the way—
And the children snuggle closer around as I begin to say:

"First thing, hey there come Mister Rabbit; don't you see him work his ears?
Huh, uh! This must be a donkey—look, how innocent he appears!
There's the old black swan a-swimming—ain't she got an awful neck?
Who's this fellow that's a-coming? Why, that's old dog Tray, I guess!"

That's the way I run on, trying just to please them all I can;
Then I holler, "Now be careful—this hey there last's the bug-a-man!"
And they run and hide their faces; they ain't scared—they're letting on:
But the play ain't really over till that bug-a-man is gone.

So I just take up my banjo, and I play a little tune,
And you see them heads come peeping out to listen mighty soon.
Then my wife says, "Such a daddy just to give you such a fright!
Just go to bed, and leave him; say your prayers and say good-night."

When I get up in the morning and the clouds are big and black,
There’s a kind of warming shiver goes a‑scooting down my back;
Then I say to my old woman as I watch down the lane,
“Don’t you sort of reckon, Lizzy, that we’re going to have some rain?”

“Go on, man,” my Lizzy answers, “you can’t fool me, not a bit,
I don’t see no rain a‑coming, if you’re wishing for it, quit;
’Cause the more you think about it, and the more you pray and wish,
Why, the rain stays away the longer, ’specially if you want to fish.”

But I see her pat the skillet, and I see her cast her eye
With a kind of anxious motion towards the darkness in the sky;
And I know what she’s a‑thinking, though she tries so hard to hide.
She’s a‑saying, “Wouldn’t catfish now taste monstrous bully, fried?”

Then the clouds get black and blacker, and the thunder ’mences to roll,
And the rain, it ’mences falling. Oh, I’m happy, bless my soul!
As I look at that old skillet, and I imagine I can see
Just a slew of new‑caught catfish sizzling there for her and me.

’T ain’t no use to go a‑plowing, for the ground will be too wet,
So I head out for the big house at a mighty pace, you bet,
And old master says, “Well, Lishy, if you think it’s going to rain,
Go on fishing, it’s the weather, and I ’low we can’t complain.”

Talk about a darky walking with his head up in the air!
Have to feel mine every minute to be sure I got it there;
And the wind is cutting capers and a‑lashing through the trees,
But the rain keeps on a‑singing blessed songs, like “Take your ease.”

With my pole upon my shoulder and my worm can in my hand,
I can feel the fish a‑waiting when I strike the river’s sand;
Never mind, you horny scoundrels, needn’t swim around and grin,
I’ll be grinning in a minute when I ’mence to haul you in.

When the fish begin to nibble, and the cork begins to jump,
I’m afraid that they’ll quit biting, ’cause they hear my heart go “thump,”
Till the cork goes way down under, and I raise an awful shout,
As a big old yellow belly comes a‑gallivanting out.

Needn’t wriggle, Mister Catfish, ’cause I’ve got you just the same,
You been eating, I’ll be eating, and we neither are to blame.
But you needn’t feel so lonesome, for I’m throwing out to see
If there ain’t some of your comrades for to keep you company.

Sport, this fishing! now you’re talking, why, they ain’t no kind to beat;
I don’t care if I am soaking, legs, and back, and neck, and feet,
It’s the sport I’m looking after. It’s the pleasure and the fun,
Though I know that Lizzy’s waiting with the skillet when I’m done.

So I head out for the big houses at one mighty pace, y'all bet,
And old masters say, “Well, Lishy, if y'all think it the thing’s fixin to rain,
Go on fishing, the thing’s the weathers, and I ’low ain't complain it.”

Talk about one darky walking with hi head up in the airs!
gotta feel mine every minutes to be sure I got me the thing there;
And the winds are cutting capers and a‑lashing through the trees,
But the rain keeps on a‑singing blessed songs, like “Take your eases.”

With my pole upon my shoulder and my worm can in my hand,
I can feel the fishs a‑waiting when I strike the river sands;
Never mind, y'all horny no scoundrels, needn’t swim around and grin,
I’ll be grinning in one minutes when I ’mence to haul y'all in.

When the fishs begin to nibble, and the corks begin to jump,
I’m afraid that they’ll quit biting, ’cause they hear it my hearts go “thump,”
Till the corks go way down under, and I raise an awful shout,
As one big old yellow belly comes a‑gallivanting out.

Needn’t wriggle, Mister Catfish, ’cause I’ve got y'all just the same,
Y'all been eating, I’ll be eating, and we neither are to blame.
But y'all needn’t feel so lonesome, for I’m throwing it out to see
If there isn’t some of your comrade for to keep y'all companys.

Sport, this here fishing! now y'all’re talking, why, does they ain’t no kind to beat;
I ain't care if I am soaking it, legs, and back, and neck, and feets,
The thing’s the sports ’m looking it after. The thing’s the pleasure and the funs,

Count the stars up in the skies,
Still there seems no place
For the educated man.

In the colored nation,
Getting lightened in the head and such as that,

On your head won't fit exact,
Still there seems no place
For the educated man.

If a man can get a sight,

Where he's qualified to go.
Still there seems no place
For the educated man.

He would like a little show,

For the educated man.

Still there seems no place

As I saunter 'round the town,
And I skim my eyes around,
Where the white folks are in business everywhere,

sae_mgt_text:
It was hard times just for Christmas in our neighborhood that year;
So we held a secret meeting where white folks couldn't hear,
To discuss the situation and see what could be done
Toward a first-class Christmas dinner and a little Christmas fun.

Rufus Green, who called the meeting, rose and said: "In this here town,
And throughout the land, white folks are trying to keep us down."
He said: "They've bought us, sold us, beat us; now they abuse us because we're free;
But when they touch my stomach, they've done gone too far for me!

'Am I right?' 'You sure are, Rufus!' roared a dozen hungry throats.
'If you'd keep a mule a-working, don't you tamper with his oats.'
"That's sense," continued Rufus. "But these white folks nowadays
Have done got so close and stingy you can't live on what they pay.

"Here 'tis Christmas-time, and, folks, I'm indignant enough to choke.
Where's our Christmas dinner coming when we're almost completely broke?
I can't hardly afford a toothpick and a glass of water. Mad?
Say, I'm desperate! They'd better treat me nice, these white folks, had they!"

Well, they abused the white folks scandalous, till old Pappy Simmons rose,
Leaning on his cane to support him, on account of his rheumatism,
And said: "Children, what's that wintry wind a-sighing through the street
About your wasted summer wages? But, no matter, we must eat.

"Now, I saw a beautiful turkey on a certain gentleman's farm.
He's a-growing fat and sassy, and a-strutting to a charm.
Chickens, sheep, hogs, sweet potatoes—all the crops are fine this year;
All we need is a committee to tote the goodies here."

Well, we lit right in and voted that it was a grand idea,
And the dinner we had at Christmas was worth traveling miles to see;
And we ate a full and plenty, big and little, great and small,
Not because we were dishonest, but indignant, sir. That's all.

Mother's in the kitchen, and the door is shut;
  All the children climb and tug and sweat,
  Getting to the window, sticking there like flies,
  Every one among us just all nose and eyes.

  "What's she cooking, Isaac?"
    "What's she cooking, Jake?"
  "Is it sweet potatoes? Is it pie or cake?"
  But we couldn't make out even where we stood
  What was mother cooking that could smell so good.

  Mother spread the window, and she frowns and frowns,
  How the children come a-tumbling down!
  Then she says: "If you all keep a-peeping in,
  How I'm going to whip you, my! It will be a sin!
  Needn't come a-sniffing and a-nosing here,
  'Cause I know my business, never fear."
  Won't somebody tell us—how I wish they would!—
  What is mother cooking that it smells so good?

  We know she means business, and we dare not stay,
  Though it's mighty trying to go away;
  But we go a-trooping down the old wood-track
  Till that steaming kitchen brings us stealing back,
  Climbing and a-peeping so as to see inside.
  What on earth can mother be so sharp to hide?
  I'd just up and tell folks when I knew I could,
  If I was a-cooking things that smelled so good.

  Mother's at the oven, and I see her smile;
  Mouths must be a-watering round here for a mile;
  Then we almost holler as we hurry down,
  'Cause it's apple dumplings, big and fat and brown!
  When the door is opened, solemn like and slow,
  Wish you saw us sitting all there in a row
  Innocent and proper, just like children should
  When their mother's cooking things that smell so good.

  Just bids me in the trying hour,
    "Lay low in the wilderness."

  And all your hopes are about to drown,

Two little boots, all rough and worn,
      Two little boots!
  Oh, I have kissed them times before,
      These little boots!
  The toes seem peeping through
  This hole and saying "Boo!"
  Every time they look at you--
      These little boots.

  Remember the time he put them on,
      These little boots;
  Rose and called for them by dawn,
      These little boots;
  Then he tromped the livelong day,
  Laughing in his happy way,
  Everything he had to say,
      "My little boots!"

  Kicking the sand the whole day long,
      Those little boots;
  Good the cobbler made them strong,
      Those little boots!
  Rocks were for that baby's use,
  I did not have to stand abuse
  When you turned these champions loose,
      These little boots!

  Used to make the old cat cry,
      These little boots;
  Then you walked it mighty high,
      Proud little boots!
  Arms akimbo, standing wide,
  Eyes saying "This is pride!"
  Then the manly-baby stride!
      You little boots.

  Somehow, you don't seem so gay,
      Poor little boots,
  Since your owner went away,
      Poor little boots!
  Your bright tops don't look so red,
  These brass tips are dull and dead;
  "Goodbye," what the baby said;
      Dear little boots!

  Aren't you kind of sad yourself,
      You little boots?
  This is all his mammy's left,
      Two little boots.
  Since her baby gone and died.
  Heaven itself seems to hide
  A little bit inside
      Two little boots.

And she perfumes the breezes
With the sweetest kind of perfume.

Just as ugly as a clown;

She was flouncing double quick.

But there she wore a wig;
Dog my cats if you could tell it,
If you could I'd dance a jig;

But that called auburn hair;
Looks so beautifully slick and wavy,
Kind of you see the white folks wear.

Had it done and rolled in ribbon,
On the pompadore style;
Had those great big whut you call 'em?
Hairpins, yes, you're right, my child;
At the sides she left it bushy
To kibosh up her ears;
Cause she saw the white folks do it
For the last forty or so years.

Yes, she had on glasses, go away!

Coming down beneath her chin;

It was flowers of all kinds,

Twist her self and lift her trail,
Cause she thought she's fine, child;

Cause the Lord in heaven knows it,

Bet they needn't take this sister,

Cause it's born in all our kind folks,
To be stylish and be proud,
Never has this lady, honey,
To such darkies ever bowed.

I have been thinking about the preacher; what he said the other night,
    About it being people's duty, to keep their faces bright;
  How one ought to live so pleasantly that our temper never riles,
    Meeting everybody round us with our very nicest smiles.

  That is all right, I am not disputing a thing that sounds like fact,
    But you do not catch folks grinning with a misery in the back;
  And you do not find them smiling when they are hungry as can be,
    Leastwise, that is how human nature always seems to appear to me.

  We are most all pretty likely to have our little cares,
    And I think we are doing first-rate when we just go along and bear,
  Without breaking up our faces in a sickly sort of grin,
    When we know that in our innards we are plainly mad as sin.

  Oh, there are times for being pleasant and for going smiling round,
    Because I do not believe in people always toting round a frown,
  But it is easy enough to titter when the stew is smoking hot,
    But it is mighty hard to giggle when there is nothing in the pot.

When the sunshine shouts glory in the sky,  
And the little Johnny-jump-ups are just springing from the ground,  
Then looking round to ask each other why.  
Don't you hear those cows mooing? That's their hello to the spring;  
Aren't they looking most uncommon satisfied?  
It's enough to make a body want to open their mouth and sing  
Just to see the creatures all so sparkling-eyed.  

Why that squirrel that just ran past us, if I could not know his tricks,  
I could swear he'd got religion just today;  
And those lizards slipping back and forth among the stones and sticks  
Are wiggling 'cause they feel so awfully gay.  
Oh, I see your eyes shining though you try to make me believe  
That you aren't so monstrously happy just because you came;  
But I tell you this here weather makes it mighty hard to deceive  
If a body's soul isn't blind and deaf and dumb.  

Robin whistling over yonder as he builds his little nest;  
What do you reckon that he saying to his mate?  
He's saying that he loves her in the words she knows the best,  
And she looks mighty pleased at what he state.  
Now, Miss Lucy, that old robin surely got his share of sense,  
And the hen-bird got her mother-wit for true;  
So I think if you'll excuse me, for I do mean no offense,  
There's a lesson in those birds for me and you.  

I'm building up my cabin, and I've vines above the door  
Fit to keep it sheltered from the sun;  
Gonna have a little kitchen with a regular wooden floor,  
And there'll be a back veranda when it's done.  
I'm waiting for you, Lucy, take the example of the birds,  
That's loving and inviting everywhere.  
I can't tell you that I love you in the robin's music words,  
But my cabin's talking for me over there!
